BRUSSELS, Oct 28 : Meta announced on Wednesday that it was indefinitely delaying the rollout of its new commercial terms following concerns from publishers and digital advertisers, in a move that could stave off potential regulatory action. EU and UK antitrust authorities have received complaints about the new terms, which publishers and digital advertisers said would give Meta an unlimited right to use their content for its AI services. Meta has rejected the claims. "We've heard publishers' feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders," Meta said in a statement. "We're committed to getting this right, and we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we'd delay implementation of the updated terms. Until then our existing terms remain in place," added Meta.

Source: Reuters

Oct 28 : Oracle expects free cash flow to turn positive in the second half of fiscal 2028 and exceed $30 billion in fiscal 2029 as capital spending declines, CFO Hilary Maxson said, offering some relief to investors concerned about its hefty AI outlays. Shares of the company, down by around a third so far this year, jumped more than 8 per cent in afternoon trading on Wednesday. Speaking at the cloud and database company's investor day, Maxson said Oracle would begin self-funding its growth in fiscal 2029 and would limit additional capital raises to $20 billion through fiscal 2030. Oracle has become a focal point of investor worries about the soaring cost of AI infrastructure because it lacks the deep revenue base of cloud giants such as Microsoft and Amazon and relies heavily on a single customer, loss-making ChatGPT maker OpenAI. For fiscal 2030, the company forecast revenue of more than $225 billion, an adjusted operating margin above 40 per cent and adjusted earnings of more than $21 per share. It reaffirmed its fiscal 2027 forecast of more than $90 billion in revenue and adjusted earnings of $8.10 per share.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON, Oct 28 : Scientists using a Chile-based telescope have identified an icy object orbiting beyond Pluto that may join our solar system's small roster of dwarf planets. Researchers said the candidate, named 2026 ED138, has a diameter estimated at between roughly 370 and 930 miles (600 and 1,500 km) and is orbiting about 46 times farther from the sun than Earth. By way of comparison, Pluto orbits at an average of about 40 times farther from the sun than Earth. The object was spotted using the new Vera C. Rubin Observatory, on the summit of the Cerro Pachón mountain in central Chile. The telescope is a joint initiative of the US National Science Foundation and US Department of Energy. Further observations are needed to confirm that the object is a dwarf planet.

If confirmed, 2026 ED138 would join five other dwarf planets recognized by the International Astronomical Union, the global authority on classifying celestial bodies. Those are Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake, all of which orbit beyond the outermost planet Neptune, and Ceres, located in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Based on the current data, 2026 ED138 would be among the largest of the dwarf planets. "For me, what this demonstrates is that many exciting discoveries remain to be made with the Rubin Observatory and other telescopes," said astrophysicist Matt Holman of the Center for Astrophysics, Harvard & Smithsonian, who first spotted 2026 ED138. Pluto long was considered the solar system's ninth and outermost planet, but was reclassified by the International Astronomical Union as a dwarf planet in 2006 because it did not meet the organization's formal definition of a planet. Pluto and the new dwarf planet candidate reside in a frigid region of the solar system populated by various icy bodies. There are still questions about the size and composition of 2026 ED138. To be considered a dwarf planet, an object must possess sufficient mass for its own gravity to pull it into a round shape. 2026 ED138 appears to have sufficient mass for that, but more observations are needed. "The main thing we need to do is to establish the physical size of 2026 ED138," Holman said. "When we observe with Rubin, we are seeing the sun's light reflected from the object," Holman said. "A smaller, more reflective object would show the same amount of light as a larger, less reflective object. Fortunately, by looking at longer wavelengths, with an observatory like ALMA, we can detect the light emitted by the object itself," which is helpful in measuring an object's size. ALMA, or the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, is a powerful telescope also based in Chile. The discovery was announced at a scientific meeting in Spokane, Washington.

Source: Reuters

(Corrects paragraph 2 to reflect that NVision has raised $120 million from public and private sources, not $155 million) By Stephen Nellis SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 28 : German startup NVision on Wednesday published a paper in the scientific journal Nature showing a new way to make quantum computing chips that would borrow from the widespread manufacturing techniques currently used in smartphone displays. Startups and tech giants such as Microsoft and IBM alike are racing to build quantum computers that hold the promise of solving problems that would take conventional machines thousands of years. But NVision, which has raised $120 million in funding from public and private sources such as Abbott Laboratories, made the discovery published on Wednesday while working in an entirely different field: improving medical devices.

The company had developed a machine that can zap special sugar molecules until the spin of their electrons aligned. The aligned spins make the sugars a thousand times easier for MRI machines to see, which in turn helps identify cancer cells that eat the sugars far faster than healthy cells. In the research published Wednesday, NVision showed that its technology can also work on organic molecules similar to those used in organic light-emitting diode (OLED) displays widely used in the electronics business. NVision used AI to simulate hundreds of candidate molecules and then physically synthesized about 40 of them until it found one that could be laid down in a thin layer over a chip made with conventional technology to create a quantum chip.  "We found this 'Goldilocks' molecule," Ilai Schwartz, NVision's chief technology officer, told Reuters in an interview. NVision also said on Wednesday that it is partnering with US-based chipmaker HyperLight to make its first chips. NVision CEO Sella Brosh said that the company plans to build an entire quantum computer rather than sell only its specialized molecules. "We want to do the whole thing, to fabricate the chips, to deposit the molecules, to do all the error correction on top of it," Brosh said in an interview. "Eventually, what we will sell is a rack-ready computer."

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON, Oct 28 : Anthropic told California Governor Gavin Newsom that government officials should be able to seek court orders blocking the release of AI models that pose a "serious risk" to the public, according to an October 15 letter that echoed the company's earlier policy proposals. Anthropic itself has faced government restrictions on its AI systems. The Trump administration in June ordered Anthropic to immediately restrict foreign access to its cyber-capable Mythos 5 and Fable 5 models, citing national security concerns. The US Commerce Department later lifted the order.  "When a review finds a model poses a serious risk, the government should be able to ask a court to block it," the letter to Newsom said.  An Anthropic spokesperson confirmed the letter is authentic. The California governor's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Anthropic submitted the recommendations after the governor in September convened a panel of artificial intelligence experts to develop proposals for AI safety requirements. The company also said it opposes requirements that developers build "kill switches" capable of shutting down entire AI models in the event a company loses control over their actions. Instead, Anthropic supports more targeted interventions, such as disabling a problematic AI agent or cutting off a specific customer's access to a model, according to the letter, saying they would be more effective. A bipartisan group of US senators in September were debating legislation that would give the US government the power to block the release of certain AI models that are deemed unsafe, Reuters reported, and companies would be able to challenge that decision in federal court. Congress left for its pre-election break shortly after, and lawmakers have not moved forward on that proposal.  US House lawmakers in July proposed the "AI Kill Switch Act," which would give US officials the power to order AI firms to shut down models that put human life or the economy at risk.  Anthropic is preparing for a US initial public offering. The listing would represent one of the most consequential stock market debuts in years, potentially reshaping benchmark indexes, investor flows and the broader narrative driving US equities. Politico first reported the details of the letter.

Source: Reuters

Oct 28 : Prediction markets are seeing massive trades for Anthropic contracts after the AI giant's IPO filing, even as retail stock traders await the official opening bell likely next month. The binary "yes" or "no" bets in prediction markets are influencing the way retail investors speculate on high-profile IPOs, allowing traders to wager on aspects such as the closing prices and its listing venue without the need to buy shares. "Prediction market interest in Anthropic's IPO is the financial equivalent of people lining up outside the Apple Store before a new iPhone release," said Michael Ashley Schulman, a partner at wealth management and financial advisory firm Cerity Partners. Earlier this week, Anthropic took a major step toward going public by unveiling its IPO filing. The listing could value the AI lab behind the Claude models at between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion, Reuters has reported.

On Polymarket, more than a dozen markets have sprung up around the IPO, where traders are placing bets on its fundraising haul, listing exchange and debut valuation. Rival Kalshi is also drawing bets on everything from which bank will lead the offering to which sector index providers will classify Anthropic in. Combined, the markets have attracted tens of millions of dollars in volume. "It is a healthy sign of robust interest and the wagers placed may help the market zero in on its eventual public market opening price," said Schulman. Prediction markets allow users to buy and sell contracts tied to the outcome of real-life events, with prices fluctuating as traders weigh the odds of the different outcomes. Once largely tied to politics and economic data, the platforms are increasingly moving into traditional Wall Street turf, offering tens of thousands of markets on stock moves, company data and other corporate events that often drive shares, Reuters reported last month. IPO investing, however, has long been dominated by deep-pocketed institutional investors. Although retail participation has expanded in recent years, including around Elon Musk's SpaceX listing, issuers still allocate only a small portion of offerings to individual investors. "The Anthropic IPO is going to be a crucial litmus test about both individual and institutional investors' appetite for AI," said Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers. The Polymarket contract on the timing of Anthropic's IPO had drawn $6 million in trading volume as of 9:30 a.m. ET (1330 GMT) on October 28. A separate market on the AI company's closing market capitalization had attracted about $3 million. "Prediction markets are clearly becoming an integral part of many investors' approach to financial risk management and speculation," Sosnick said.

Source: Reuters

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 28 : Amazon cut about 250 jobs on Wednesday in its devices and services unit after weeks of product rollouts including new Kindle e-readers and tablet computers. The company confirmed the cuts after a Reuters inquiry. "We've made the difficult decision to eliminate a small number of roles," a spokesperson said without elaborating. The cuts affected no more than 250 jobs, said a person familiar with the matter, primarily in software development.  The layoffs will help the company "operate more efficiently and better align with our product roadmap," the spokesperson said. Amazon on Wednesday also announced a new Alexa-powered alarm clock and photo frame. As is the company's custom, text messages and emails were sent to workers early Wednesday morning. One seen by Reuters was from Cherie Robinson, a human resources vice president in devices and services, saying the company had undergone "a thorough review of our structure" resulting in the need for cuts. Earlier this month, Amazon pared about 1,000 jobs in its core retail division. The company reports its third-quarter earnings after the market close on Thursday.

Oct 28 : The heavyweights of the AI industry are facing a reckoning on Wall Street, reflecting concerns over who will bear the cost of the artificial intelligence buildout that has fueled much of this year's stock market gains. Anthropic revealed paperwork for its initial public offering on Monday, paving the way for a share sale reportedly worth $100 billion as early as next month. Meta also unveiled a plan this week that could bring it as much as $97.5 billion through equity offerings over the coming months. The markets will also await signs of fundraising plans when Microsoft and Alphabet report earnings later on Wednesday.

By pressing ahead with their enormous funding plans, the biggest AI players are wagering that investors' fear of missing out on future returns will outweigh their fear of overpaying for them. AI stocks accounted for nearly 75 per cent of the S&P 500 index's return in the first half of 2026, according to an analysis by Carson Group. "The growth of the AI ecosystem over the last several years is quite astounding," said Ehren Stanhope, chief investment strategist at Franklin Templeton's Canvas. "The idea that such large firms can compound earnings at triple digits for multiple years seems to defy the laws of economics." But Wall Street's reaction in recent weeks suggests ambition is no longer enough to get investors to open their wallets. Meta's shares have fallen more than 11 per cent since it unveiled plans last week to create a new class of stock to fund share sales and reported its first quarterly cash burn in more than a decade. While Anthropic's soaring revenue helped ease AI growth concerns, its mounting losses have raised fresh questions. The company's net loss widened to $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026 from $13 billion a year earlier. "Not even Anthropic will get a blank check," said Matt Kennedy, senior strategist at Renaissance Capital. The funding demands are coming amid growing circular financing arrangements, in which money invested in AI companies can flow back to their investors through spending on computing infrastructure and services. SMALLER FIRMS FEEL THE HEAT Companies that are relatively small but carry heavy debt are in a more bleak position. CoreWeave has seen its bond yields soar, raising questions about how much it would have to pay in interest when it raises debt next. "The danger (for CoreWeave) is the next loan. And how soon CoreWeave needs it matters as much as the price," said Matthew Tuttle, founder and CEO of Tuttle Capital Management. Last week, CoreWeave's shares hit their lowest since May 2025 as concerns about its reliance on debt grew. The stock has rebounded around 10 per cent so far this week, but "a company surviving and its old shareholders winning are two different outcomes," Tuttle added. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk recently said neocloud companies could face significant consolidation and failures. He ruled out any acquisition of a neocloud company by SpaceX, saying such a deal would be "pointless." Still, this year's AI capex by Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Oracle and Microsoft would likely equal their cumulative spend since the November 2022 launch of ChatGPT, according to data from J.P. Morgan. "In effect, the Street appears to be underwriting the AI data center monetization case," wrote Dubravko Lakos-Bujas, the brokerage's head of global markets strategy.

SAP uses more than 70 AI models from providers including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. "The goal is healthy margins as scale grows, not an absolute reduction in AI expenditure," SAP said in answers to Reuters questions. Customers are also paying closer attention to where AI models come from. Asam said government agencies and companies in regulated industries increasingly ask specific requirements and exclude models based on origin, while European customers increasingly demand local solutions.

WASHINGTON, Oct 28 : Global commodity prices are set to surge 23 per cent in 2026, the World Bank said on Wednesday, citing rising energy prices and disruptions to cargo shipping during the Middle East war, grain shipment problems in the Black Sea and high demand for safe-haven assets such as gold. Oil, natural gas, food and metals prices all rose sharply this year as global shocks mounted, the World Bank said in its latest Commodity Markets Outlook. It said the situation could worsen if the conflict in the Middle East ratcheted up and damage to Russian oil infrastructure continued. Commodity prices were expected to ease by 7 per cent next year, it said, but continued shocks - including forecasts for the worst El Niño weather effect since 1950 - could keep food commodity prices elevated, raising the specter of higher inflation and tighter monetary policy. The global economy was more vulnerable to future supply shocks at the moment. Global oil stocks have been depleted during the war in the Middle East, and global oil supply is expected to drop 5.2 per cent in 2026, the biggest drop in four decades outside the 2020 global recession, the bank said.

"Commodity markets are being hit by several major shocks at once," said Ayhan Kose, the World Bank’s deputy chief economist. "Higher energy costs and trade disruptions are driving up prices across a broad range of commodities, threatening to worsen inflation, food insecurity, and economic growth." The bank released its twice-yearly report on Wednesday, two days before foreign ministers from the world's 20 largest economies are due to gather in Atlanta, Georgia for a meeting that will focus on the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine. Kose said the World Bank was focused on protecting the world's poorest people and supporting low-income countries already grappling with heavy debt burdens. The bank had already provided $8.7 billion in low-cost loans and other aid to 25 countries affected negatively by the war in the Middle East, the report said. This included 10 countries that retooled existing programs to cover crisis-related expenses, and 19 that had tapped new resources, with some using both. The report, released twice a year, said global energy prices surged 32 per cent in 2026, reaching their highest level since 2022's invasion of Ukraine by Russia. With oil output down, Brent oil prices were expected to remain elevated in the near term, averaging $92 per barrel for the year. Prices would be even higher if oil demand were not forecast to drop 2.5 per cent this year, the third-largest drop behind the 2020 COVID shock and the 1980 oil crisis. It said food commodity prices were set to rise just over 10 per cent in 2026 due to grain shipment disruptions caused by hostilities between Russia and Ukraine in the Black Sea, and another 7 per cent-plus in 2027, for a cumulative increase of nearly 18 per cent. An adverse scenario that coupled a record El Nino, more Black Sea grain shipment disruptions, escalation in the Middle East conflict and ongoing damage to Russian oil infrastructure could drive food prices 12 per cent higher than expected, it said. That could trigger a food crisis like the one seen in the early 2010s, when more than 40 million additional people were pushed into extreme poverty, the bank noted. Fertilizer prices were expected to rise 14 per cent in 2026, due to a surge in urea prices, returning to 2025 levels in 2027. Metals prices were projected to rise 25 per cent and hit a new high in 2026, with aluminum, copper and tin all setting new records as a result of supply disruptions and strong demand from investments in renewable energy, electric vehicles and data centers, the bank said. Precious metals prices were projected to surge by 40 per cent in 2026, amid elevated demand for safe-haven assets triggered by geopolitical and policy uncertainty, with some moderation seen in 2027.

Source: Reuters

LONDON, Oct 28 : Finance minister John Healey on Wednesday unveiled plans in his budget to support the development of data centres in Britain, linking the measure to the government's artificial intelligence and national security objectives. Healey said the government would launch a new British Data Centre Covenant requiring operators to invest in local communities, create jobs and protect water supplies, in return for priority grid connections and, where necessary, permission to build on-site power generation. "Built on sovereignty and security, I want to ensure that the British people can benefit from the huge potential upsides of AI," Healey told parliament. He said the aim was to keep sensitive data used by public services and the armed forces in Britain as the use of artificial intelligence expands. Healey also announced an AI Challenge Prize to encourage the use of AI in public services and funding to support workers adapting to technological change.

FAST

WASHINGTON, Oct 28 : Mars is a dusty place. Dust is circulated by everyday winds, whirlwinds called dust devils and larger dust storms raging at local, regional and global scales. Dust is a factor that must be addressed in any human mission to Mars, and new data from a NASA rover is revealing just how much of a challenge it may present. NASA's Perseverance rover, operating in and around an area called Jezero Crater in the Martian northern hemisphere since landing in 2021, has detected the finest particles of dust to date on Earth's planetary neighbor. It documented ultrafine particles as small as around 100 nanometers wide, about 500 times thinner than a human hair. "A smaller particle size does not necessarily make dust more dangerous, but smaller particles do have a higher potential to penetrate deeper into the human body and are harder for the body to clear," said planetary scientist Scott VanBommel of Washington University in St. Louis, a member of the Perseverance science team and lead author of a study describing the findings in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. "Like any substance, toxicity depends on dose and duration. Martian dust contains silica, iron compounds and chlorine compounds such as perchlorate, which are known to be harmful at high enough doses on Earth," VanBommel said.

Perseverance measured dust particles that stuck to rover hardware including spacesuit materials carried aboard the six-wheeled robotic vehicle with the intent to observe how they hold up in the planet's harsh environment. Previous measurements resolved Martian dust particles down to about 3 micrometers in diameter. But Perseverance's Planetary Instrument for X-ray Lithochemistry, or PIXL, documented two categories of particles even smaller. Along with the ultrafine particles, there was a category of fine particles of less than 2.5 micrometers in diameter, or 30 times thinner than a strand of hair.     Such tiny particles could be small enough to penetrate an astronaut's lungs, enter the bloodstream and potentially damage vital organs. Another concern is that the Martian environment and dust's physical properties could degrade spacesuit and habitat materials over time.     With this in mind, Perseverance carries samples of possible spacesuit materials such as the manufactured fiber Vectran and the protective coating Teflon, each about three-quarters of an inch (20 mm) square. "We don't have evidence that the dust damaged the spacesuit materials, just that the materials tended to interact with dust differently," VanBommel said. "Vectran appeared to hold larger dust particles, with the greatest prevalence on the underside of its weave. The Teflon sample held less dust, but the dust it held was finer, reflecting differences in how electrostatic properties can preferentially adhere particles of different sizes to each material." ASTRONAUTS ON MARS NASA is looking to send astronauts to Mars as early as the 2030s. "These findings will help inform the design of future human support systems for crewed Mars missions, including the choice of suit and habitat materials and cleaning methods that work at sub-micron particle sizes. They also add to the guidelines and protocols NASA has established for toxicological risk," VanBommel said. "How much dust reaches a habitat will depend largely on how suits and airlocks are designed, and that work is ongoing. NASA is currently studying suitports — docking stations for spacesuits — and dual-chamber airlocks, as well as other concepts, to keep dust out of living areas," VanBommel said. NASA has experience with the effects of dust from the Apollo astronaut moon landings from 1969 to 1972. Lunar dust degraded outer spacesuit layers, damaged seals and scratched visors. It also may have been associated with symptoms resembling hay fever among some astronauts. But Mars dust differs from lunar dust. "On the moon, dust is generated largely by surface impacts, including by micrometeorites. With no atmosphere or wind to wear them down, lunar particles stay sharp and angular. Most of the concern about lunar dust comes from its shape, whereas for Martian dust its chemistry and particle size are the primary concerns," VanBommel said. Mars dust arises primarily from the planet's fine-grained basaltic rocks. Weathering of the particles makes them less abrasive. "The active wind environment mixes it globally, giving it a rather uniform composition. That same environment rounds the particles and gradually breaks them into smaller particles through collisions," VanBommel said. Perseverance's focus has been on searching for signs of ancient Martian microbial life. But NASA also has used it to prepare for human missions. "The results from this study do not mean Mars is too dangerous for humans. Mars dust is a hazard that has to be designed for, in the same way radiation and distance from Earth are," VanBommel said.

Source: Reuters

Oct 28 : Telenor's efforts to persuade mobile customers to pay more for network quality and security services could face a new test from AI shopping agents expected to focus heavily on price, executives said on Wednesday. The Norwegian operator's "more-for-more" strategy adds benefits to subscriptions to encourage higher spending. Its task is to make those extras count when customers compare offers. AI agents would be "to a large degree price driven", CEO Benedicte Schilbred Fasmer told Reuters, saying the benefits beyond connectivity needed to be clear to customers. That would add another dimension to an already competitive market. Telenor lost 22,000 mobile subscriptions in Norway in the third quarter, while mobile revenue per user rose 2.7 per cent year on year.

CFO Torbjorn Wist argued in a call with analysts that prices were already transparent and that coverage, capacity and security would remain a "strategic moat". He also saw agents as a possible route to customers, provided Telenor could exchange information with them. The concern extends beyond telecoms. Payments firm Adyen told Reuters in August that merchants feared losing direct customer relationships and repeat business as shoppers increasingly turned to AI chatbots. Fasmer said Nordic identification requirements would keep people involved in subscription changes. Asked about competition in Norway, she remained confident in the existing strategy, although its pace could slow in some markets. "But we don't think we've run out of road on the more-for-more strategy," she said. Telenor is building a more Nordic-focused business, adding services such as security alongside connectivity while reducing its exposure in riskier Asian markets.

Oct 28 : Amazon.com on Wednesday unveiled five new Alexa-powered devices including a redesigned Echo Show 16 smart display and a photo frame with built-in Alexa, as it pushes its latest version of the voice assistant into customers' homes. Here are more details: • The Echo Show 16, which has a 16-inch screen, built-in Fire TV and Amazon's first Echo Show camera with night vision, is available for pre-order from $499.99 • A new Echo Studio speaker with a built-in camera, which lets Alexa recognize objects held up to it and lets users check on a room remotely, costs $249.99
